Note

What are the best exercises for arthritis?

Note

A mix usually works best: low-impact aerobic activity such as walking, cycling or swimming, strengthening exercises for the muscles around painful joints, and gentle movement for flexibility and balance such as tai chi or yoga. NICE recommends therapeutic exercise as a core treatment for osteoarthritis, and UK guidance for adults is to build towards 150 minutes of moderate activity a week with strengthening on at least two days. The best exercise is one you can keep doing.

Exercise today: start here

  1. Check the red flags in the box below. If any apply, get help before you exercise.
  2. Warm up for a few minutes: march on the spot, roll your shoulders or circle your ankles.
  3. Pick one routine for the joint that bothers you most: knee, hip, , or .
  4. Do a few slow repetitions at a comfortable effort. You should be able to talk while you move.
  5. Check how you feel tomorrow and adjust using the pain guide below. Little and often beats one big session.

In pain right now? Start with the pain relief guide, then come back to gentle movement.

Red flags: stop and get help

Do not exercise the joint, and call NHS 111 or your GP for a same-day appointment if:

  • one joint suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially with a fever or feeling unwell
  • you take medicines that lower your immunity, such as methotrexate or biologics, and you have signs of infection
  • a joint is very painful after a fall or injury, or you cannot put weight on a leg

Stop and call 999 if you get chest pain or tightness, severe breathlessness, or feel faint while exercising.

Is it safe? How to read pain when you exercise

Exercise is unlikely to harm your joints. NICE advises explaining this to people with osteoarthritis, along with the fact that some extra aching at first can happen.

  • Mild ache that settles within a day: usually fine. Carry on and build up slowly.
  • Pain much worse the next day, or more swelling: do fewer repetitions or a shorter session next time. Do not stop altogether.
  • Sharp, catching pain, or a joint that gives way: stop that exercise and ask a physiotherapist.

Flare days: do less, not nothing

  • Swap strengthening for gentle range-of-movement: bend and straighten the joint slowly a few times every hour.
  • Cut the time or repetitions, rather than stopping. Complete rest makes stiffness worse.
  • Use heat on stiff joints, or a wrapped cold pack on a hot, swollen joint, for up to about 20 minutes.
  • Build back up over a few days once the flare settles. Use the flare-up guide and the printable flare action plan.

When to see your GP or a physiotherapist

  • pain or swelling keeps getting worse after exercise, even when you do less
  • you are not sure which exercises are safe after an injury, an operation or a joint replacement
  • you have heart or lung problems, or feel dizzy or breathless with gentle activity
  • a joint locks, gives way or you are falling

In many areas you can refer yourself to NHS physiotherapy without seeing a GP: check your GP surgery or local NHS website. Waiting already? See help while you are on a waiting list.

Chair-based movement for older adults

As the UK population ages, maintaining mobility and independence becomes a paramount concern for older adults and the people supporting them. Exercise is often called the closest thing we have to a “magic pill” for healthy ageing — but for many people living with arthritis, traditional high-impact workouts are not realistic because of joint degeneration, balance issues or chronic pain. This is where low-impact movement, and chair exercises in particular, become genuinely useful. Short, accessible routines — often as little as ten minutes a day — meet people where they are and remove the intimidation of a long gym session.

Chair exercises address several of the physiological changes that come with ageing. First, they reduce the risk of falls and injury by giving people a stable base while they work. By staying seated, you can focus on the muscular action without the cognitive load of worrying about balance. Second, they are good for the heart. You do not need to run a marathon to elevate your heart rate. Arm circles, seated marching, torso twists and gentle boxing motions, performed in sequence, raise circulation, help manage blood pressure and support long-term cardiovascular health.

The benefits extend well beyond the physical. Regular activity releases endorphins, the body’s natural mood lifters, which can help offset the isolation, anxiety or low mood that sometimes accompany later life. Light resistance work using small hand weights or resistance bands during a chair workout pushes back against sarcopenia — the age-related loss of muscle mass. Preserved muscle strength is what allows older adults to keep doing the Activities of Daily Living (ADLs) that protect autonomy: cooking, washing, dressing, getting on and off the toilet, and managing stairs.

For people living specifically with arthritis, gentle movement keeps the joints lubricated and the surrounding tissues flexible, which reduces the morning stiffness that often triggers further inactivity and pain. The key is consistency rather than intensity. A short daily routine is far more useful than a punishing weekly session that leaves you sore for days. Build the habit first, then add reps, light resistance or a few extra minutes as you adapt. Proper form matters more than effort — slow, controlled movement is what protects joints and tendons.

This is general information, not medical advice. Speak to a GP, physiotherapist or rheumatologist before starting any new exercise programme, especially if you have heart, balance or joint conditions.

For carers and family

Encourage little and often rather than doing everything for the person. Stand nearby for balance work, use a sturdy chair without wheels, and keep a note of what they managed so you can both see progress. Stop and get help if they become breathless, dizzy or have chest pain, or if a joint becomes hot, red and swollen. Looking after someone? You may be entitled to a carer's assessment.

What is the best diet for arthritis?

Note

The NHS advises a healthy, balanced diet and keeping to a healthy weight, because extra weight strains your joints. NICE NG226 says any weight loss helps people with osteoarthritis who are overweight, and NG100 encourages people with rheumatoid arthritis to follow Mediterranean principles: more fruit, vegetables, fish and plant oils, less meat.

Key clinical takeaways

  • No diet cures arthritis; a balanced diet supports exercise, medicines and your other treatment.
  • If you have osteoarthritis and are overweight, any weight loss helps, and losing 10% of body weight is likely better than 5% (NICE NG226).
  • NICE NG100 encourages Mediterranean diet principles for rheumatoid arthritis: more fruit, vegetables, fish and plant oils, less meat.
  • Don't drink too much alcohol, and follow your rheumatology team's limits if you take methotrexate.

Frequently asked questions

What is the best diet for arthritis joint pain?

Note

The best diet for arthritis is the Mediterranean diet — rich in vegetables, fruit, wholegrains, olive oil, oily fish, nuts and pulses. NHS and Arthritis UK (formerly Versus Arthritis) guidance supports a Mediterranean-style pattern for general health and joint-friendly eating. For osteoarthritis, gradual weight loss where appropriate (often discussed as around 5–10% of body weight with a clinician) can ease load on weight-bearing joints — this is educational, not a personal target.

Why Diet Matters for Arthritis

The relationship between diet and arthritis is one of the most researched areas in rheumatology. While no single food can cure arthritis, mounting evidence demonstrates that what you eat can significantly influence inflammation levels, pain intensity, joint stiffness, disease activity and even the effectiveness of medications. Reviews of Mediterranean-style and anti-inflammatory dietary patterns (including work summarised for clinicians in journals such as Nutrients) suggest diet can support lower pain and inflammatory markers for some people — effects vary, and diet does not replace prescribed treatment.

For people with osteoarthritis, diet also plays a critical role in weight management. Excess weight is the single most modifiable risk factor for OA: every 1 kg of body weight lost reduces the load on each knee by approximately 4 kg with every step (Messier et al., 2013). For overweight individuals with knee OA, losing just 5–10% of body weight can produce clinically meaningful reductions in pain and improvements in function.

The Mediterranean Diet: The Gold Standard

The Mediterranean diet is the most extensively studied dietary pattern for arthritis and chronic inflammation. It consistently outperforms other diets in clinical trials for reducing inflammatory markers, joint pain and cardiovascular risk — which is elevated in people with inflammatory arthritis.

Want a plan to follow this week? See the focused 7-day Mediterranean eating plan for arthritis — UK shopping list, recipes and what to eat freely, weekly and rarely.

Core Principles

  • Abundant vegetables and fruits — aim for 7+ portions daily, focusing on colourful varieties rich in antioxidants (berries, leafy greens, tomatoes, peppers, beetroot)
  • Wholegrains — oats, brown rice, wholemeal bread, quinoa, bulgur wheat
  • Healthy fats — extra virgin olive oil as the primary fat source (rich in oleocanthal, which has ibuprofen-like anti-inflammatory properties)
  • Oily fish — at least 2 portions per week (salmon, mackerel, sardines, trout) for omega-3 fatty acids EPA and DHA
  • Legumes and pulses — lentils, chickpeas, beans — excellent protein and fibre sources
  • Nuts and seeds — walnuts (highest plant omega-3), almonds, flaxseeds, chia seeds
  • Herbs and spices — turmeric, ginger, garlic, oregano, rosemary — many have documented anti-inflammatory properties
  • Moderate dairy — yoghurt and cheese in moderation; fermented dairy supports gut health
  • Limited red meat — no more than 1–2 portions per week; processed meats avoided
  • Limited sugar and refined carbohydrates — these promote inflammation

A landmark 2023 trial in Annals of the Rheumatic Diseases found that RA patients following a Mediterranean diet for 16 weeks experienced a significant reduction in DAS28 scores (a composite measure of disease activity) compared to controls, with improvements in fatigue and quality of life.

Key Anti-Inflammatory Foods

Omega-3 Fatty Acids

Omega-3s are the most well-evidenced dietary component for arthritis. EPA and DHA — found primarily in oily fish — are converted into anti-inflammatory compounds called resolvins and protectins that actively help resolve inflammation. A 2017 meta-analysis in the British Journal of Clinical Pharmacology found that fish oil supplementation (2–4 g/day of combined EPA/DHA) significantly reduced joint pain, morning stiffness and NSAID use in RA patients.

Best food sources:

  • Salmon (wild-caught) — 2.2 g omega-3 per 100 g
  • Mackerel — 2.6 g per 100 g
  • Sardines — 1.5 g per 100 g
  • Trout — 1.0 g per 100 g
  • Walnuts — 2.5 g ALA (plant omega-3) per 30 g
  • Flaxseeds — 6.7 g ALA per 30 g (ground for absorption)
  • Chia seeds — 5.0 g ALA per 30 g

Recommendation: Aim for 2 portions of oily fish per week plus daily plant sources. If you don't eat fish, consider an algae-based omega-3 supplement (providing EPA/DHA directly).

Turmeric and Curcumin

Turmeric's active compound, curcumin, is one of the most extensively studied natural anti-inflammatory agents. It works by blocking NF-ÎºB — a master regulator of inflammation — and inhibiting COX-2 and LOX enzymes (similar mechanisms to NSAIDs like ibuprofen). A 2016 systematic review and meta-analysis published in the Journal of Medicinal Food concluded that 1,000 mg/day of curcumin significantly reduced pain and improved function in knee OA patients.

Key considerations:

  • Curcumin has poor bioavailability on its own — pairing with black pepper (piperine) increases absorption by up to 2,000%
  • Study curcumin products differ from cooking turmeric — ask a clinician or pharmacist before using concentrated supplements
  • Some trials show curcumin provides comparable pain relief to diclofenac with fewer side effects
  • Consult your doctor if taking blood thinners or diabetes medication, as curcumin may interact

Ginger

Ginger contains gingerols and shogaols — bioactive compounds with anti-inflammatory and analgesic properties. A 2015 meta-analysis of 5 randomised controlled trials found that ginger supplementation (500–1,000 mg/day) significantly reduced OA pain compared to placebo. Fresh ginger can be used in cooking (1–2 cm fresh root daily) or as a tea.

Berries and Antioxidant-Rich Foods

Berries — particularly blueberries, strawberries, cherries and blackcurrants — are rich in anthocyanins, powerful antioxidants that reduce oxidative stress and inflammation. Tart cherry juice has been specifically studied for gout, where it has been shown to reduce uric acid levels and flare frequency. Other antioxidant-rich foods include dark leafy greens (kale, spinach), beetroot, sweet potatoes and dark chocolate (70%+ cocoa).

Foods That May Worsen Arthritis

While individual responses vary, certain foods are consistently associated with increased inflammation and worsened arthritis symptoms:

  • Processed and ultra-processed foods — ready meals, crisps, biscuits, processed meats (bacon, sausages, ham) — high in advanced glycation end products (AGEs) that promote inflammation
  • Added sugars — fizzy drinks, sweets, cakes — trigger inflammatory cytokine release
  • Refined carbohydrates — white bread, white pasta, pastries — spike blood sugar and insulin, promoting inflammation
  • Excessive alcohol — increases uric acid (worsens gout) and systemic inflammation
  • Excessive omega-6 fatty acids — found in sunflower oil, corn oil and many processed foods — when consumed in excess relative to omega-3, these promote pro-inflammatory pathways
  • Trans fats — hydrogenated oils found in some margarines and commercial baked goods
  • Excessive red meat — particularly processed meats, which contain nitrites and saturated fats

Supplements: What the Evidence Says

Glucosamine and Chondroitin

These are the most widely used OA supplements in the UK. Evidence is mixed: a 2018 Cochrane review found glucosamine provides small, uncertain benefits for pain compared to placebo. Chondroitin alone showed similarly modest effects. Combined glucosamine/chondroitin may offer slightly better outcomes, but the evidence is not strong enough for NICE to recommend routine use.

Collagen (Hydrolysed)

Emerging research suggests hydrolysed collagen peptides (10 g/day) may modestly reduce joint pain and stiffness in OA. A 2019 meta-analysis in International Orthopaedics found statistically significant improvements in pain and function, though effect sizes were small. Collagen is generally well-tolerated.

Vitamin D

Vitamin D deficiency is extremely common in the UK (affecting up to 1 in 5 adults) and is associated with worse arthritis outcomes. The health service recommends all UK adults take a 10 mcg (400 IU) vitamin D supplement daily during autumn and winter. People with inflammatory arthritis may benefit from higher doses (discuss with your doctor).

Fish Oil (Omega-3 Supplements)

If you don't consume enough oily fish, a high-quality fish oil supplement providing 1–3 g of combined EPA/DHA daily is the most well-evidenced supplement for arthritis. Look for purified, sustainably sourced products with high EPA content. Algae-based alternatives are equally effective for vegetarians and vegans.

Gut Health and Arthritis

Emerging research links the gut microbiome to inflammatory arthritis. An imbalanced gut microbiome (dysbiosis) may trigger or worsen autoimmune responses in conditions like RA and PsA. To support gut health:

  • Eat 30+ different plant foods per week — diversity feeds diverse beneficial bacteria
  • Include fermented foods — kefir, sauerkraut, kimchi, live yoghurt, miso
  • Consume prebiotic fibre — garlic, onions, leeks, asparagus, bananas, oats
  • Limit artificial sweeteners and emulsifiers — these may disrupt gut bacteria

Weight Management for Joint Health

Maintaining a healthy weight is arguably the most impactful dietary intervention for OA. Evidence-based strategies include:

  • Focus on nutrient-dense, high-satiety foods — vegetables, protein, wholegrains and healthy fats keep you fuller for longer
  • Avoid crash diets — they lead to muscle loss, which worsens joint instability
  • Aim for gradual weight loss — 0.5–1 kg per week is sustainable and preserves muscle mass
  • Combine dietary changes with regular low-impact exercise — walking, swimming, cycling
  • Consider portion control rather than food restriction — using smaller plates and mindful eating techniques

The NICE guidelines for OA (NG226) specifically recommend weight loss as a first-line treatment alongside exercise, stating it should be offered before medication.

Practical Tips for UK Shoppers

  • Budget-friendly options — tinned fish (sardines, mackerel), frozen berries, dried lentils and tinned chickpeas are just as nutritious as fresh alternatives
  • Read labels — look for traffic-light labels; aim for green on fat, sugar and salt
  • Buy seasonal UK produce — cheaper and more nutritious; farmer's markets often have better value
  • Batch cooking — prepare soups, stews and curries in bulk and freeze portions
  • Joint-friendly cooking — use electric can openers, lightweight pans and adaptive kitchen utensils from organisations like the Arthritis Action or OT referral

Common types of foot and ankle arthritis

  • Big toe arthritis (hallux rigidus) — the most common foot osteoarthritis. The big toe stiffens and hurts when you push off; a bony bump often appears on top of the joint.
  • Midfoot arthritis — deep ache across the top of the foot, worse on uneven ground or after previous injury.
  • Ankle osteoarthritis — less common than knee or hip OA but often disabling; many cases follow an old fracture, dislocation or repeated severe sprain.
  • Rheumatoid or psoriatic arthritis in the feet — small toe joints, ball-of-foot pain, swelling and deformity; footwear and early rheumatology care matter.

Gout also loves the big toe — see our gout guide if flares are sudden, hot and intensely painful.

What are the symptoms?

  • Pain with every step — or a deep ache that builds after walking
  • Morning stiffness — brief in osteoarthritis, often longer in inflammatory arthritis
  • Swelling — around the ankle, midfoot or big toe joint
  • Reduced push-off — especially with hallux rigidus
  • Instability or fear of falling — stiff, painful ankles alter balance (see our falls prevention guide)
  • Shoe struggle — standard footwear presses on bony bumps or swollen toes

What causes it?

  • Previous injury — ankle fractures and severe sprains are the leading risk for ankle OA
  • Age and cumulative load — cartilage wear in the big toe and midfoot after 50
  • Inflammatory disease — rheumatoid and psoriatic arthritis frequently involve the feet
  • Biomechanics and footwear — high heels, narrow toe boxes and uncorrected flat or high-arch patterns
  • Family history — especially for hallux rigidus and Heberden-like patterns in the toes

Daily tasks most affected

Walking on uneven ground84% Standing for long periods78% Finding comfortable shoes72% Climbing stairs61% Getting going after sitting55%

What are the best exercises?

Keep the ankle and toes moving within a comfortable range. Warm the foot in a basin of warm water for 10 minutes first. Full routine: foot and ankle arthritis exercises.

Range of motion

  • Ankle circles — 10 each way, both feet
  • Alphabet tracing — write letters in the air with your big toe
  • Toe spreads and towel scrunches — strengthen intrinsic foot muscles

Strength and balance

  • Heel raises — hold a counter, rise onto toes, lower slowly. Build to 2 sets of 10–15
  • Band dorsiflexion — pull toes toward you against a light band
  • Single-leg stance — near a wall; progress toward 30 seconds each side

Avoid: high-impact jumping, barefoot walking on hard floors during flares, and forcing a painful big toe into deep bend.

Footwear, orthotics and lifestyle

  • Wide, deep toe box and adjustable fastenings for day-to-day swelling
  • Rocker or stiff sole for big toe arthritis to reduce joint bend at push-off
  • Removable insoles so NHS or private orthotics can fit
  • Low heel — under about 2.5 cm reduces forefoot pressure
  • Pair footwear changes with the same anti-inflammatory pattern in our Diet Hub

How is it treated in the UK?

Self-management

  • Supportive shoes and activity pacing
  • Daily mobility and balance routine
  • Topical NSAID gel around the painful joint if suitable for you
  • Heat before activity; short ice packs after a flare

NHS pathway

  • GP — assessment, X-rays or blood tests when inflammatory disease is possible
  • Podiatry — biomechanics, orthotics, footwear advice
  • Physiotherapy — graded loading and balance (self-referral in many areas)
  • Orthopaedics — injections, fusion or replacement when conservative care is not enough
  • Rheumatology — if RA, PsA or other inflammatory disease is suspected

If referrals are delayed, our waiting-list help guide covers what you can do meanwhile.

When should you see your GP?

  • Foot or ankle pain lasting more than a few weeks
  • Warm, red or markedly swollen joint
  • New deformity, ulcers, or numbness in people with diabetes
  • Falls or near-falls linked to unstable ankles
  • Known inflammatory arthritis with a new foot flare

Early signs include morning stiffness in the ankle or big toe, a deep ache with the first steps of the day, swelling around the joint after walking, and shoes that suddenly feel tight over a bony bump on top of the big toe joint. Swimming is one of the most recommended activities for managing ankle arthritis. It helps reduce stiffness, strengthen the muscles around the ankle joint, and improve your overall mobility — all with minimal joint impact.   • Improves cardiovascular fitness
  • Increases range of motion
  • Reduces stiffness and swelling
  • Strengthens muscles around joints

1. Ankle Circles in Water

10 each direction

Hold pool edge, rotate each ankle slowly in water.

2. Toe Raises in Water

3 × 10

Stand in shallow water, rise onto toes, lower slowly.

3. Kick Board Kicks

5 minutes

Hold kickboard, flutter kick gently to mobilise ankles.

/conditions/knee-arthritis:
What is knee arthritis?

Knee arthritis is the gradual wearing down of the cartilage that lines the knee joint. The knee has three compartments — medial (inside), lateral (outside) and patellofemoral (under the kneecap) — and arthritis can affect any combination of them.

As cartilage thins, the bones underneath thicken, small bony spurs (osteophytes) form, and the lining of the joint can become inflamed. This produces the familiar mix of pain, stiffness and swelling.

How common is it in the UK?

Around 4.11 million people in the UK live with knee osteoarthritis, making it the single most common cause of mobility loss in older adults.

What are the symptoms of knee arthritis?

  • Pain on stairs — particularly going downstairs, when load on the patellofemoral joint peaks
  • Morning stiffness — usually under 30 minutes; longer suggests inflammatory arthritis
  • Swelling — a "boggy" feeling around the kneecap, often worse after activity
  • Crepitus — grinding or clicking when bending the knee
  • Giving way — the knee buckles momentarily, usually because the quadriceps have weakened
  • Reduced range — difficulty fully straightening or bending the knee

What causes knee arthritis?

  • Age — most cases develop after 45
  • Body weight — every extra pound transmits ~4 lb of force through the knee
  • Previous injury — meniscus tears, ACL ruptures and fractures multiply risk 3–6×
  • Occupation — repeated kneeling, squatting or heavy lifting (carpet fitters, tilers, farmers)
  • Sex — women are roughly 1.5× more likely to develop knee OA after menopause
  • Alignment — bow-legs (varus) load the medial compartment; knock-knees (valgus) load the lateral

Symptom impact (typical patient survey)

Pain on stairs88% Morning stiffness76% Swelling after activity64% Sleep disturbance52% Giving way38%

What are the best exercises for knee arthritis?

NICE lists exercise as a core treatment for everyone with knee OA — not optional. The most effective programmes combine quadriceps strengthening with low-impact aerobic work.

Strengthening

  • Straight-leg raises — the safest way to load the quadriceps without bending the knee. 3 sets of 10, daily.
  • Wall sits — start at 10 seconds, build to 60. Stop above 90° of knee bend if painful.
  • Step-ups — onto a low step, controlling the lowering phase. 2 sets of 10 each leg.
  • Glute bridges — strong glutes reduce knee load by improving hip mechanics.

Low-impact cardio

  • Stationary cycling — set the saddle high enough that the knee is almost straight at the bottom
  • Swimming or aqua-aerobics — buoyancy removes 70–90% of body weight from the joint
  • Walking — start with 10-minute blocks, build to 30; cushioned shoes only

What diet helps knee arthritis?

Weight loss is the single most powerful non-surgical treatment for knee arthritis. A 5% reduction in body weight typically delivers a 20–30% drop in knee pain. Pair calorie control with the Mediterranean pattern covered in our Diet Hub:

  • Oily fish twice a week (salmon, mackerel, sardines)
  • Plenty of vegetables, berries, nuts, olive oil and whole grains
  • Limit ultra-processed food, sugary drinks and excess alcohol

Straight-leg raises and wall sits — start small, build slowly.

Cycle

Cycling is easier on the knee than running or jumping.

Weight

Losing 5% of body weight often eases knee load a lot.

Ice

Ten minutes after activity if the knee is warm or swollen.

How is knee arthritis treated?

Self-management

  • Daily strengthening programme
  • Weight management
  • Heat before activity, ice after
  • Walking pole on the opposite side to offload the painful knee

Medical treatments

  • Topical NSAIDs (ibuprofen or diclofenac gel) — first-line per NICE for knee OA
  • Oral NSAIDs / paracetamol — short courses where topical isn't enough
  • Corticosteroid injection — short-term flare relief, typically lasting 4–12 weeks
  • Physiotherapy — supervised exercise plus manual therapy

Surgery

Total or partial knee replacement is considered when pain disturbs sleep, severely limits daily activity, and at least 3–6 months of conservative treatment has not worked. Around 100,000 knee replacements are performed in the UK each year, with 90%+ still functioning well at 15 years.

How do DMARDs and biologics differ for rheumatoid arthritis?

Biologics are a type of disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drug (DMARD). This guide compares conventional DMARDs, such as methotrexate, with biological DMARDs for inflammatory arthritis. JAK inhibitors are a separate group called targeted synthetic DMARDs, not biologics. Conventional DMARDs can help rheumatoid arthritis and peripheral joint disease, but are not recommended for purely axial spondyloarthritis affecting the spine.

Updated 11 July 2026

Frequently asked questions

Last reviewed 11 July 2026

Biologics are a type of disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drug (DMARD). This guide compares conventional DMARDs, such as methotrexate, with biological DMARDs for inflammatory arthritis. JAK inhibitors are a separate group called targeted synthetic DMARDs, not biologics. Conventional DMARDs can help rheumatoid arthritis and peripheral joint disease, but are not recommended for purely axial spondyloarthritis affecting the spine.

Conventional DMARDs

  • How it works: Broadly damp down the immune system. Methotrexate is the anchor drug; others include sulfasalazine, hydroxychloroquine and leflunomide.
  • Best for: First-line treatment for rheumatoid, psoriatic and juvenile arthritis. Often used long-term.
  • Common side-effects: Nausea, mouth ulcers, hair thinning, raised liver enzymes, low blood counts. Reversible with dose changes.
  • UK healthcare availability: Freely prescribed on the UK healthcare system, usually started by rheumatology and monitored with regular blood tests.
  • Typical UK cost: Very cheap — methotrexate tablets cost the UK healthcare system pennies per week.

Biologics

  • How it works: Use engineered proteins to target parts of the immune response, such as TNF, IL-6, IL-17 or B cells. JAK inhibitors are targeted synthetic DMARDs, not biological medicines.
  • Best for: Selected people with active inflammatory arthritis when other suitable treatments have not controlled it. The treatment pathway depends on the condition and medicine.
  • Common side-effects: Infections and injection-site reactions are possible; other risks depend on the medicine. JAK inhibitors have separate safety warnings and should not be treated as biologics.
  • UK healthcare availability: Prescribed by specialist rheumatology under medicine- and condition-specific eligibility criteria, with ongoing monitoring.
  • Typical UK cost: £8,000–£15,000+/year — usually free to eligible UK healthcare patients; biosimilars have reduced the price significantly.

How the two families really differ

Conventional DMARDs are old-school immune suppressants: they slow down a wide range of immune activity, which is why they work but also why they need blood monitoring. Methotrexate — the most-used arthritis medicine in the world — is safe and effective for most people at once-weekly doses.

Biological DMARDs target parts of the immune response. Examples include adalimumab, etanercept and infliximab (TNF inhibitors), tocilizumab (an IL-6 inhibitor), secukinumab (an IL-17 inhibitor) and rituximab (which targets B cells). They are given by injection or infusion. JAK inhibitors, such as tofacitinib and baricitinib, are tablets in the separate targeted synthetic DMARD group.

How the UK healthcare system decides who gets what

The NHS treatment pathway depends on the diagnosis, disease activity, previous treatments and the particular medicine. In rheumatoid arthritis, conventional DMARDs are usually tried before a biological treatment. The same sequence should not be assumed for every inflammatory arthritis condition.

For purely axial spondyloarthritis, conventional DMARDs are not recommended because they do not effectively treat spinal disease. They may still be used for peripheral arthritis, such as swollen joints in the arms or legs. Biological medicines or JAK inhibitors may be considered by a specialist when appropriate for axial disease.

Side-effect trade-offs

DMARDs need regular blood tests (fortnightly at start, then every 8–12 weeks) to catch liver, kidney or blood-count problems early. Common day-to-day side-effects — nausea, mouth ulcers, tiredness the day after methotrexate — often improve with folic acid, dose splitting or an anti-sickness tablet.

Biological medicines can increase infection risk, including reactivation of infections such as TB. Screening and monitoring depend on the medicine and your health history. JAK inhibitors are a different medicine group with separate warnings, including cardiovascular problems and blood clots. Ask your rheumatology team what to do if you develop an infection; do not apply one stopping or restarting rule to every medicine.

Cost and access

For the individual patient, both are free on the UK healthcare system if criteria are met (though there's a prescription charge in England for DMARD tablets unless you're exempt). To the UK healthcare system, however, biologics cost thousands per patient per year — mitigated significantly by the rise of biosimilars, which are cheaper 'generic' versions with equivalent effect.

Privately, methotrexate and other DMARDs can be prescribed for a few pounds a month; biologics privately cost hundreds to a few thousand a month, so almost all UK patients access them through the UK healthcare system.

Which is 'better'?

For most newly-diagnosed rheumatoid arthritis, methotrexate remains the anchor drug — often combined with a short course of steroids to bridge until it kicks in. Roughly half of patients get durable low disease activity or remission on DMARDs alone.

For those with persistent activity or specific features (like severe skin psoriasis or axial disease), biologics are transformative and now expected in the UK healthcare system treatment pathway. Increasingly, rheumatologists tailor the choice of biologic to the disease pattern and personal factors like pregnancy, cardiovascular risk and needle tolerance.

Key takeaways

  • Biologics are DMARDs too. This comparison is conventional versus biological DMARDs.
  • JAK inhibitors are targeted synthetic DMARD tablets, not biologics.
  • Conventional DMARDs are not recommended for purely axial spinal disease, although they may help peripheral arthritis.
  • Side effects, infection precautions and monitoring depend on the individual medicine and your health history.
  • Biosimilars have made biologics far more affordable for the UK healthcare system.
  • The goal for either family is remission or low disease activity, not just pain relief.

This is general information, not medical advice. Discuss Conventional DMARDs and Biologics with your GP, rheumatology team or pharmacist before starting, stopping or switching treatment.

/arthritis-mental-health:
Living with arthritis is not just a physical experience. Persistent pain, fatigue and uncertainty take a real toll on mood, sleep and identity. This evidence-based guide covers what to look out for, what helps, and where to get support — for you and the people around you.

Mental health impact of arthritis

Arthritis is a whole-life condition. Alongside swollen joints and morning stiffness come broken sleep, cancelled plans, uncertainty about the future and, for many people, a slow renegotiation of who they are at work and at home. Those losses are real, and they show up in mood, motivation and concentration long before anyone calls it a mental health problem.

The strain tends to build in three ways. Pain itself is processed in brain regions that also handle emotion, so persistent pain lowers mood and lowers the threshold at which the next pain feels unbearable. Fatigue shrinks the activities that normally restore you. And unpredictability — not knowing whether tomorrow is a good day or a flare — makes planning, socialising and working feel risky, so people withdraw.

Naming this early matters. Distress that is recognised and treated responds well; distress that is dismissed as "just part of arthritis" tends to deepen and can make pain, disability and treatment adherence measurably worse.

Depression in arthritis

Depression is more common in people with inflammatory and degenerative arthritis than in the general population, and it is frequently missed because low mood, tiredness and poor sleep are all assumed to be joint symptoms. The distinguishing features are persistence and pervasiveness: low mood or loss of pleasure on most days for two weeks or more, along with hopelessness, guilt, loss of appetite, difficulty concentrating, or thoughts that life is not worth living.

Treatment works. UK Talking Therapies services accept self-referral in England — you do not need to go through your GP — and offer cognitive behavioural therapy adapted for long-term conditions. Antidepressants can help, and some, such as duloxetine or low-dose amitriptyline, are used in chronic pain in their own right; your GP can discuss whether one is suitable alongside your arthritis medication.

Tell your rheumatology team as well as your GP. Uncontrolled inflammation drives mood symptoms, so a flare that is treated properly often lifts mood as a side effect, and knowing you are struggling may change how the team plans your care.

Anxiety & pain

Anxiety in arthritis usually attaches to something specific: fear of a flare, fear of falling, fear of a joint replacement, fear of losing a job or a benefit. That vigilance is understandable, but it has a cost — muscles stay braced, breathing gets shallow, sleep becomes light, and the nervous system reads ordinary sensations as danger. Pain feels sharper as a result.

The most common downstream problem is avoidance. Stopping the walk, the swim or the social event reduces anxiety in the moment and increases disability over months, because deconditioning makes the next attempt harder. Graded, paced return to activity — small, boring, repeatable amounts — breaks that cycle more reliably than waiting until you feel confident.

Practical anchors help: slow breathing with a longer out-breath, a written flare plan so a bad day has a script rather than a panic, and pacing that budgets activity across the week instead of overdoing good days and paying for it afterwards.

Coping strategies

Pacing is the foundation. Break tasks into shorter blocks with planned rests, alternate heavier and lighter jobs, and stop before the pain forces you to. The aim is a steady, sustainable level rather than the boom-and-bust pattern most people fall into.

Keep the parts of life that carry meaning. Adapt rather than abandon: a shorter walk, a seated version of a hobby, an online rather than in-person meet-up. Activity that matters to you protects mood far better than rest does.

Sleep and movement are treatments, not extras. A consistent wake time, a cool dark bedroom, timing pain relief so it covers the first part of the night, and daily low-impact movement all improve pain and mood together. Alcohol is a poor sleep aid and worsens both.

Finally, be specific when you ask for help. "I need someone to do the weekly shop on Thursdays" is easier for family to act on than "I am struggling", and it protects you from the exhaustion of explaining an invisible condition over and over.

Mindfulness & meditation

Mindfulness does not switch pain off. What trials in chronic pain consistently show is a change in the relationship with pain: less pain-related distress, less interference with daily life, and lower anxiety scores. For many people that is the difference between a day lost and a day managed.

Start small and unglamorous. Ten minutes of guided body scan or breath-focused practice most days, at a time you can protect, beats an ambitious plan you abandon. Free NHS-endorsed apps and audio guides are widely available, and gentle mind-body movement such as tai chi or chair yoga combines the same attentional practice with the joint-friendly exercise arthritis needs anyway.

If your mind wanders constantly, nothing has gone wrong — noticing and returning is the practice. If sitting still increases distress, which sometimes happens with trauma or severe anxiety, use a movement-based version and mention it to your GP or therapist.

Support resources

Your GP is the usual first stop and can refer, prescribe and sign-post. In England you can also self-refer to NHS Talking Therapies without seeing your GP first; equivalent services exist across Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland.

Rheumatology teams often include specialist nurses with a telephone advice line — use it during a flare rather than waiting for the next appointment. Occupational therapy can reduce the daily friction that grinds mood down, and physiotherapy can rebuild confidence in movement after a long avoidant period.

Peer support matters more than people expect, because it removes the work of explaining. Our own community pages and moderated groups are one route; local hospital and council-run pain management programmes are another.

If pain is dominating life, ask about a pain management programme — these are group, multidisciplinary and specifically designed to improve function and mood rather than to eliminate pain.

When to seek help

Book a routine GP appointment if low mood, anxiety or sleep problems have lasted more than two weeks, if you have stopped doing things you used to enjoy, if you are drinking more, or if you are taking more pain relief than prescribed to cope with how you feel.

Seek help the same day if you feel unable to keep yourself safe, if you have thoughts of harming yourself, or if you are so distressed you cannot function. Call 111 for urgent advice, Samaritans free on 116 123 at any hour, or text SHOUT to 85258.

Call 999 if you or someone else is in immediate danger, or has taken an overdose. Asking for help early is not an overreaction — it is the same principle as treating a flare before it becomes a hospital admission.

What tai chi is, and why it suits arthritis

Tai chi is a gentle form of exercise that started as a Chinese martial art. It uses slow, flowing movements, controlled shifts of body weight from one leg to the other, and relaxed, steady breathing. Because the movements are slow and low-impact, and can be done standing or seated, it suits many people with painful or stiff joints who find other exercise difficult.

For arthritis, tai chi combines several things that help in one activity:

  • Gentle movement of the joints through a comfortable range, which helps stiffness.
  • Leg strength, from holding slightly bent knees and shifting weight slowly.
  • Balance and confidence, from controlled weight shifting and stepping.
  • Relaxation, from slow breathing and focus, which can help people cope with long-term pain.

What the evidence and guidance say

NICE guideline NG226 recommends therapeutic exercise, tailored to the person, as a core treatment for everyone with osteoarthritis, combining muscle strengthening and general aerobic fitness. It does not prescribe one type of exercise; tai chi can be a good choice if it suits you and you enjoy it, alongside strengthening exercises such as our knee exercises for osteoarthritis. Research studies suggest tai chi may help improve pain and physical function in knee osteoarthritis, and a 2019 Cochrane review of exercise for preventing falls in older people living in the community found that tai chi probably reduces the rate of falls. Evidence for rheumatoid arthritis is more limited, but tai chi appears to be safe for people whose condition is stable.

Tai chi is not a cure for arthritis, and it works best as part of a wider plan that includes strengthening, staying active, and any treatment you have been prescribed.

Before you start

  • Check with your GP or physiotherapist first if you have had a recent fall, recent surgery or joint replacement, dizziness, or a heart or lung condition.
  • Wear loose, comfortable clothes and flat, supportive shoes, or practise in socks only on a non-slip floor.
  • Have a sturdy chair or worktop next to you for support.
  • Keep your knees soft and only slightly bent. Shallow stances are fine and are easier on painful knees and hips.
  • Move within comfort. Tai chi should not cause sharp pain. A little muscle tiredness at first is normal.

The five core movements, step by step

These written steps go with the short demonstrations in the movement library on this page. Move slowly, breathe naturally, and stay within comfort.

1. Rooted stance

Stand with your feet hip-width apart and toes pointing forward. Soften your knees slightly, let your arms hang loosely, and imagine a thread gently lifting the top of your head. Breathe slowly for 5 to 10 breaths. This is the starting and finishing position for every sequence.

2. Weight shift

From the rooted stance, slowly move your weight onto your right foot without lifting either foot, then slowly back to the middle and over to the left. Keep your head level and your knees soft. Do 5 to 10 slow shifts each way. Hold a worktop if you need to.

3. Cloud Hands

With your weight centred, raise your hands softly in front of your body, palms facing in, at about chest height. Turn gently from the waist to one side, letting the arms follow, then turn back the other way, as if your hands are drifting past clouds. Keep the movement small at first and below shoulder height. Repeat 5 to 8 times each way.

4. Brush Knee

Step one foot forward a short, comfortable distance and slowly shift your weight onto it. As you do, sweep one hand down past the front knee and gently push the other hand forward at chest height. Shift back, bring the foot in, and repeat on the other side. Keep steps short if your knees or hips are painful. Repeat 3 to 5 times each side.

5. Closing posture

Return to the rooted stance. Slowly raise your arms in front of you to chest height as you breathe in, then lower them as you breathe out, letting your weight settle evenly through both feet. Repeat 3 times.

A 10-minute home session

  1. Warm-up (2 minutes): gentle shoulder rolls, wrist circles, ankle circles and marching on the spot.
  2. Rooted stance and breathing (1 minute).
  3. Weight shifts (2 minutes).
  4. Cloud Hands (2 minutes).
  5. Brush Knee (2 minutes), or seated arm movements if standing is difficult.
  6. Closing posture (1 minute).

Note how your joints feel later that day and the next morning. Mild muscle tiredness is normal; if joint pain is worse for more than a day, make the movements smaller next time.

Finding a class in the UK

Learning from a teacher helps you get the movements right and keeps you motivated. Look for classes described as gentle, beginner, seated, or for older adults or people with long-term conditions. Leisure centres, community centres, libraries and some NHS and community falls-prevention services run classes. Before you join, tell the teacher about your arthritis and any joint replacements, and ask whether movements can be adapted. Your GP practice may also be able to link you to local activities through social prescribing.

When to stop and get medical help

Stop and rest if you feel dizzy, unusually breathless, or have sharp joint pain.

  • Call 999 if you have chest pain, severe breathlessness, or feel faint and it does not settle with rest.
  • Call NHS 111 or go to A&E if a joint suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially with a high temperature, or if you fall and cannot get up or bear weight.
  • See your GP or a physiotherapist if you have frequent falls or near-falls, pain that is getting steadily worse, or you are not sure which movements are safe after surgery.

Cervical osteoarthritis (arthritis in the neck) causes stiffness, aching and reduced rotation that can make driving, sleeping and looking up uncomfortable. These seven exercises — used by UK physiotherapy teams and aligned with NICE guidance for joint pain — keep the neck mobile, build the deep stabilising muscles and ease the upper-back tension that often drives symptoms.

Stop any movement that causes sharp pain, dizziness or symptoms travelling into the arms. Seek medical advice if you have numbness, weakness, balance changes or pain that wakes you at night — these need proper assessment, not exercise alone.

Who these exercises are for

  • Cervical osteoarthritis (wear-and-tear of the neck joints)
  • General neck stiffness from desk work or poor posture
  • Rheumatoid arthritis affecting the cervical spine (under physio guidance)
  • Recovery from a neck strain once acute pain has settled
  • People wanting to maintain neck mobility as they age

The seven exercises

  1. 1. Chin tucks

    Posture reset · eases upper-neck pressure

    Sit tall. Without tilting your head, gently draw your chin straight back as if making a double chin. Hold 3 seconds, release. Keep your eyes level.

    Reps: 2 sets of 10, twice daily

  2. 2. Slow neck rotations

    Range of motion · seated

    Looking forward, slowly turn your head to the right as far as is comfortable. Hold 2 seconds, return to centre, then turn to the left. Move within a pain-free range.

    Reps: 8 turns each side, once or twice daily

  3. 3. Side-to-side tilts

    Loosens the sides of the neck

    Drop your right ear towards your right shoulder (don't lift the shoulder). Hold 5 seconds, return to centre, repeat on the left. Stop short of any pinching.

    Reps: 6 tilts each side

  4. 4. Forward and back flexion

    Front-to-back mobility

    Tuck the chin to the chest gently, hold 3 seconds. Return to neutral, then tilt the head back a small amount (avoid forcing it). Move slowly.

    Reps: 8 reps, once daily

  5. 5. Shoulder rolls

    Releases the muscles that anchor the neck

    Lift both shoulders towards your ears, roll them back and down in a smooth circle. Reverse direction halfway through.

    Reps: 10 rolls each direction

  6. 6. Isometric neck press

    Strengthens deep neck stabilisers

    Place your palm against your forehead. Press your head gently into your hand without letting either move — hold 5 seconds. Repeat with the hand on each side of the head and the back.

    Reps: 5 holds in each direction

  7. 7. Upper trapezius stretch

    Eases tension that drives neck pain

    Sit on your right hand to anchor the shoulder down. Tilt your left ear towards your left shoulder; use the left hand to add a very gentle pull. Hold 20 seconds. Swap sides.

    Reps: 2 holds each side

How often should I do them?

Once or twice a day is enough. Start with chin tucks, rotations and shoulder rolls for the first week, then layer in the stretches and isometric press as your neck tolerates them. Five minutes daily is more useful than a long session twice a week.

If your job involves long hours at a screen, set a reminder to do chin tucks and shoulder rolls every hour — most flare-ups in the neck come from sustained postures, not from heavy use.

Frequently asked questions

What exercise is good for arthritis in the neck?

Chin tucks, slow neck rotations and gentle side-to-side tilts are the safest starting point for cervical osteoarthritis. They keep the joints lubricated, ease morning stiffness and don't load the spine. Build up to isometric strengthening and upper-trapezius stretches once the basics feel comfortable.

Should I exercise when my neck is in a flare?

Yes — but stay with gentle range-of-motion work only (chin tucks, slow rotations within a small range). Avoid loaded stretches, end-range bending and any movement that triggers radiating pain into the arm. If symptoms last more than two weeks, see a GP or physiotherapist.

Are neck circles safe?

Full rolling circles aren't recommended for arthritic necks — the backward portion compresses the small facet joints. Use rotations, tilts and forward flexion as separate movements instead.

When should I see a doctor?

Get medical advice promptly if you have pins and needles, weakness or numbness in the arms or hands, problems with balance or bladder control, or pain that wakes you at night. These can signal nerve involvement that needs proper assessment.

Short, practical everyday tips for living with arthritis in the UK — movement, food, pacing and sleep.

Key Takeaways

  • 1.Everyday tips work best when they are short, realistic and easy to repeat
  • 2.Use them as a menu, not a checklist to finish in one day
  • 3.Start the morning with a glass of water and a few gentle stretches before getting busy
  • 4.Stand or walk for a minute each hour if you sit for long periods

Everyday tips work best when they are short, realistic and easy to repeat. Use them as a menu, not a checklist to finish in one day.

1. Start the morning with a glass of water and a few gentle stretches before getting busy.

2. Stand or walk for a minute each hour if you sit for long periods.

3. Keep joint-friendly snacks ready — walnuts, berries, yoghurt, vegetable sticks.

4. Pace chores: one room or one task, then a short rest.

5. Warmth helps many people — layers, warm showers, or a heat pack before activity.

6. Note flares in a simple diary so you can spot patterns and discuss them with your GP or rheumatology team.

7. Ask about occupational therapy aids if dressing, cooking or bathing is becoming hard.

8. Protect sleep: a regular bedtime and a cool, dark room make a real difference to pain and mood.

Small changes, kept up, usually beat ambitious plans you cannot sustain.

Daily Living 1 min read Health & Wellness

Practical UK habits that ease stiffness and support everyday life with arthritis.

Key Takeaways

  • 1.Movement — change position often; short walks and light stretches keep joints from locking up
  • 2.Food — favour oily fish, nuts, fruit, vegetables and whole foods; cut back on ultra-processed snacks where you can
  • 3.Hydration — water helps joints move more comfortably
  • 4.Rest — consistent sleep and pacing reduce next-day flares

Living well with arthritis is less about perfect routines and more about small, repeatable habits that protect your joints day to day.

Joints need regular, gentle movement, steady hydration, and enough rest to recover. Long spells of sitting, skipping meals, or pushing through every good day often make stiffness and fatigue worse.

Focus on four building blocks:

Movement — change position often; short walks and light stretches keep joints from locking up

Food — favour oily fish, nuts, fruit, vegetables and whole foods; cut back on ultra-processed snacks where you can

Hydration — water helps joints move more comfortably

Rest — consistent sleep and pacing reduce next-day flares

At home, favour ergonomic tools (larger-handled cutlery, jar openers, perching stools) and plan tasks in short bursts. On tougher days, scale activity rather than stopping altogether — Arthritis UK (formerly Versus Arthritis) and NHS advice both emphasise staying as active as you safely can.

These habits will not replace prescribed treatment, but they make daily life more manageable alongside your care team.
